aer_racers.title: Aer Racers
aer_racers.subtitle: A Ghibli-inspired multiplayer pod racing game for Nintendo Switch
aer_racers.intro: Aer Racers is a multiplayer pod racing game developed during my third year at SAE Institute of Geneva. Built on a custom C++ engine for Nintendo Switch, I led a team of 25 people as Project Manager, Lead Designer, and Lead Gameplay Programmer.
aer_racers.highlight_1: Custom C++ engine targeting Nintendo Switch
aer_racers.highlight_2: Team of 25 people (10 Artists, 2 Audio, 13 Programmers)
aer_racers.highlight_4: Local multiplayer with up to 4 players
aer_racers.blogposts_description: Dive deeper into the technical aspects of Aer Racers development:
aer_racers.blog_postmortem_desc: Complete analysis of the project: team organization, design decisions, gameplay programming, and lessons learned.
aer_racers.blog_menu_desc: How I implemented the menu system, game state management, and player selection screen using enum-based architecture.
aer_racers.blog_waypoint_desc: Technical deep-dive into the waypoint system used for player positioning and race placement calculations.
aer_racers.concept_text: Our game is a multiplayer pod racing game where players can reach high speeds but must carefully manage their velocity to avoid obstacles. The unique control scheme uses each joystick to control a separate rotor of the spaceship, creating an engaging and skill-based racing experience.
aer_racers.ref_swe1r: Our main reference. Inspired the high-speed gameplay and open level design.
aer_racers.ref_mk8: Inspired the simple UI design and race level design principles.
aer_racers.ref_wipeout: Inspired the smooth camera behavior and vehicle reactions.
aer_racers.ref_porco: Studio Ghibli's Porco Rosso inspired our spaceship designs with a 1930s aesthetic.
aer_racers.ref_rime: Rime inspired our low-poly visual style and colorful environments.
aer_racers.role_lead: Coordinated team of 25, managed communications, organized weekly meetings
aer_racers.role_designer: Defined game concept, mechanics, and directed level design
aer_racers.role_programmer: Implemented 3Cs, menu systems, waypoint system, and game management

aer_postmortem.title: Aer Racers Post Mortem
aer_postmortem.subtitle: Complete analysis of the project from start to finish
aer_postmortem.context_text: This project was developed at the SAE Institute of Geneva during my third year of bachelor in Games Programming. The objectives were to create a game on a custom Game engine in C++ that would run on the Nintendo Switch.
aer_postmortem.team_intro: For the project, we were 4 main members who worked on the project from start to end:
aer_postmortem.team_total: The entire team counted 25 people working on the project:
aer_postmortem.constraints_tech_intro: Technical constraints given by our teacher:
aer_postmortem.constraint_1: Use the Neko engine (custom game engine developed by our teacher and ourselves)
aer_postmortem.constraint_2: Develop a game for the Nintendo Switch
aer_postmortem.project_text: Our project "AerRacers" is a multiplayer pod racing game where the player can go very fast but has to be careful about obstacles. The player has to manage speed - the ship's movements are directly controlled by the joycons joysticks, each stick moving a rotor from the spaceship.
aer_postmortem.organization_text: We had 5 months to develop this project (September 17th 2020 - May 07th 2021). Every week, we held meetings to track everyone's progress:
aer_postmortem.meeting_1: Wednesday: Meeting with the 4 main team members
aer_postmortem.meeting_2: Thursday: Meeting with our teacher Elias Fahran
aer_postmortem.lead_project_text: As Lead Project, I had to communicate with every team member and manage the leads. I was also responsible for communication with external members. At the beginning, we accumulated delays because members met problems with their tasks. To catch up, we reorganized our planning in December and cut some features. After that, we managed to meet our deadlines.
aer_postmortem.ref_mk8_text: We were inspired by Mario Kart 8 for the simple UI and level design.
aer_postmortem.ref_swe1r_text: Our main reference. We got inspired by the speed and open levels.
aer_postmortem.ref_wipeout_text: We got inspired by the smooth camera and vehicle reactions.
aer_postmortem.ref_porco_text: We got inspired by the Porco Rosso ships with a 1930s look.
aer_postmortem.ref_rime_text: Inspired us for the low poly look and colorful environments.
aer_postmortem.concept_intro: We decided to develop our game around these basic rules:
aer_postmortem.concept_mechanics: We thought about mechanics like destructible ships, boosts, and health bars, but only kept local multiplayer due to development delays.
aer_postmortem.level_design_text: We worked on level design using Unity Engine with two different scenes: a Playground for testing 3Cs and a Level Design scene for the final level.
aer_postmortem.programmer_intro: The gameplay development was split into two parts:
aer_postmortem.dev_part_2: Game features & exportation of Unity code to Neko Engine
aer_postmortem.camera_text: To make a fun camera, I had the idea to make it behave like a driver in a car. If the ship accelerates, the camera would lag behind. I imagined a spring system linking the ship and camera. The development of this system took more than 2 months due to glitching issues. In the end, we used a simpler SmoothDamp function.
aer_postmortem.neko_text: After Unity development, I worked on the Neko Engine to implement missing features. Stephen worked on Unity code implementation and Audio, while I worked on menu and game management and the waypoint system.
aer_postmortem.soft_skills_text: I learned about my strengths and weaknesses. I have strong logic skills - it's not hard for me to create working code when I know what I'm doing. I also learned that I preferred working on systems instead of gameplay features. The quarantine due to COVID-19 had a huge impact on my motivation and working efficiency.
aer_postmortem.work_skills_text: A skill I missed was knowledge in maths that could help solve simple problems. I learned that I still have a lot of work to do to be a better programmer. It's also very important to organize code well and be more curious about others' code.
aer_postmortem.lesson_1: Define game design and concept as fast as possible, especially the MVP
aer_postmortem.lesson_2: Iterate on gameplay frequently and create tests often
aer_postmortem.lesson_3: Don't stay too long on one task - ask for help early
aer_postmortem.lesson_4: Be curious about colleagues' code to understand it better
aer_postmortem.lesson_5: Ask precise questions when blocked - a 3-day problem might be solved in 10 minutes by a teammate

aer_menu.title: Menu & Game Management for AerRacers
aer_menu.subtitle: State management and UI systems in a custom C++ engine
aer_menu.context_text: We developed a video game project during our third year of bachelor at SAE Institute of Geneva in Games Programming. Our objective was to create a racing game for the Nintendo Switch, using a custom Game Engine in C++ developed by our teacher and by us. Our game "AerRacers" is a multiplayer pod racing game, where each player controls the rotors of their spaceship with the joysticks.
aer_menu.problem_text: In video games, it's very important to manage game status. That's why games have menus and game managers. In our game, we have 2 different ship models each with different textures. It was important to let players choose their ship, join the game, and manage the game status to let players win and return to the menu. To do so, I created a Menu Manager and a Game Manager.
aer_menu.section_main: Where the player can look at the credits or start the game
aer_menu.section_credits: Where the credits of each team member are displayed
aer_menu.section_selection: Where players can join the game and select their spaceship skin
aer_menu.selection_text: The Selection Screen was important because there's a bunch of spaceship models & textures created by the Game Art team. It's also where the Game Manager gets information about which ship model to load and how many players will play.
aer_menu.enum_intro: To update the state of the menu, I created several enum classes:
aer_menu.enum_menu: Used to know which part of the menu the player is in.
aer_menu.enum_pointer: Used to know which button is highlighted.
aer_menu.enum_credits: Used to know which credits page the player is viewing.
aer_menu.enum_selection: Used to know which part of selection each player is in.
aer_menu.enum_model: Used to know which model the player has selected.
aer_menu.loading_text: We decided to load every texture and model at game start using other threads of the Nintendo Switch. Since we only have one level, the level loads while the player is in the main menu. However, a problem occurred: the level loaded faster than the menu, displaying chunks before the game manager. We reorganized the loading order:
aer_menu.loading_3: Spaceships and InGame UI Loading (only when game starts)
aer_menu.game_manager_text: The game manager manages the entire game. It updates the current game status, updates the UI for each player, and checks which player has finished.
aer_menu.game_states_intro: The Game Manager uses an enum class called GameState:
aer_menu.state_waiting: Countdown before the start of the game
aer_menu.state_end: Displays the end score then loads the main menu
aer_menu.waypoint_integration: To know if each player has finished the race, the Game Manager gets information from the Waypoint Manager.
aer_menu.problem_lazy_text: I wanted to get a working system as fast as possible and then switch to another system instead of finishing lazy work like code polishing and writing credits text. This caused several problems:
aer_menu.problem_1: Code was working but not clean
aer_menu.problem_2: Missing lazy tasks accumulated and cost more time later
aer_menu.problem_3: Unclean code + missing tasks created organizational problems
aer_menu.learned_text: The development of the Menu and Game Management wasn't really hard to implement. When you have a precise idea of what you'd like to do and how, it's not very hard to implement a working system. The harder part of programming is knowing what you do and organizing your code well. Otherwise, you could get lost and lose more time than if you solved problems when they were fresh in your head.

aer_waypoint.title: Waypoint System for Player Placement
aer_waypoint.subtitle: Calculating player positions in a racing game using dot products
aer_waypoint.context_text: We developed a video game project during our third year of Bachelor at SAE Institute of Geneva. Our objective was to create a racing game for Nintendo Switch using a custom C++ Game Engine. Our game "AerRacers" is a multiplayer pod racing game where players can go very fast but must control their speed to avoid crashing.
aer_waypoint.problem_text: An important feature in a multiplayer racing game is knowing player positioning. There are several ways to get it - you could imagine systems using triggers or chunks - but I decided to use a waypoint system for these reasons:
aer_waypoint.reason_2: Easier to implement in our engine
aer_waypoint.system_text: The waypoint system uses a waypoint map in which the player's position is calculated between waypoints. The waypoint manager keeps a target waypoint to calculate the player's position and updates the target by calculating the dot product between the vector Player-Waypoint and the vector Waypoint-NextWaypoint.
aer_waypoint.data_length: Length between this waypoint and the next
aer_waypoint.data_vector: Normalized vector to the next waypoint
aer_waypoint.player_data_intro: I store every piece of information about player positions in a structure called "PlayerPositionData":
aer_waypoint.array_placement: Keeps the players' placement in race
aer_waypoint.array_position: Keeps the dot product value for each ship
aer_waypoint.array_waypoint: Keeps the current waypoint for each player
aer_waypoint.array_count: Keeps the waypoint count for each player
aer_waypoint.max_players: The data is stored in arrays of size 4, corresponding to maximum players.
aer_waypoint.manager_intro: To manage our waypoints, I created a waypoint manager with these key functions:
aer_waypoint.func_add: Called when loading the scene to get waypoints from JSON
aer_waypoint.func_placement: Calculates player placement using position data
aer_waypoint.func_start: Starts waypoint detection and gets player data
aer_waypoint.func_restart: Restarts manager when returning to main menu
aer_waypoint.creation_intro: Before updating player positions, I had to create and store waypoints:
aer_waypoint.step_1: Place waypoints on the Unity map
aer_waypoint.step_2: Export waypoints with Unity Scene Exporter tool
aer_waypoint.step_3: Import waypoints with Neko Scene Importer tool
aer_waypoint.step_4: Place waypoints in the Waypoint Manager array
aer_waypoint.update_intro: To update player position data, we go through these steps:
aer_waypoint.update_1: Calculate the vector between ship position and waypoint for each ship
aer_waypoint.update_2: Calculate the dot product between this vector and the waypoint's normalized next vector
aer_waypoint.update_3: Check the dot product value of each ship
aer_waypoint.update_5: CalculatePlayerPlacement: Check if players have won and compare values to create placement
aer_waypoint.negative_title: Checking if the Dot is Negative
aer_waypoint.negative_text: At first, when the dot product was negative, I set the target waypoint to the previous one. The problem was that in some situations, the dot could be negative while also higher than the previous waypoint length, causing waypoint changes every frame. To solve this, I added a check when negative to verify if the dot product was higher than the previous waypoint length.
aer_waypoint.paths_text: Another situation was when the game had multiple paths. I created a boolean to check if the player had multiple next waypoints, then checked both waypoints. I also added a check to see which waypoint the player was nearest to. In the end, we decided not to implement multiple paths since it wasn't necessary for our map.
aer_waypoint.export_problem_text: One of the main problems was that it was my first time working on the Neko Engine. The most complicated part was exporting waypoints from Unity and loading them correctly. I had to look at colleagues' code, which would've been easier if I was more curious during development. For example, the x-axis was inverted in Neko Engine, and I lost time trying to fix my system when it was actually an export issue. I solved this by asking precise questions about the problems I met.
aer_waypoint.personal_text: I was sure it would be much harder to code in C++, but switching between C# and C++ wasn't very hard. I learned that I liked creating systems more than programming gameplay features, because it's easier to know what you're doing when you don't depend too much on other people's code.
